evidence.title: Managing a "responsibility vacuum" in AI monitoring and governance in healthcare: a qualitative study
evidence.outcome: Clarity of responsibility for AI maintenance and monitoring tasks
evidence.effect: Maintenance and monitoring tasks were described as poorly defined, inconsistently performed, and undervalued across healthcare systems, a 'responsibility vacuum'.
evidence.quote: This study explores the phenomenon of a "responsibility vacuum" in AI governance, wherein maintenance and monitoring tasks are poorly defined, inconsistently performed, and undervalued across healthcare systems.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether assigning named accountable owners to AI solutions reduces unaddressed failures, although 34 frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries recommend some form of it. Two qualitative interview studies suggest that responsibility for AI harms and upkeep is often unclear in practice, which shows the problem exists but not that named ownership fixes it.

perspectives.view: Zero studies compare outcomes with and without named AI owners. The two available studies are qualitative interviews (n=40 developers; n=21 experts) that describe the hazard. They cannot estimate an effect, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The endorsements reflect expert agreement rather than tested results.

Interviewees described maintenance and monitoring as poorly defined and inconsistently performed, a condition they called a responsibility vacuum. Among 40 developers, recognition of their own duty to address harms varied widely. These findings suggest that model drift or errors may go uncaught when no one is assigned, but no study shows that naming owners catches them sooner.

The interview data indicate that monitoring tasks are undervalued within health system workflows. A named owner may exist on paper while the work goes undone if time and tools are not attached to the role. No study has measured whether ownership assignments are kept current or carried out with fidelity after deployment.

The recommendation covers six responsibility areas for every AI solution, which could require multiple staff per tool as portfolios grow. The finding that upkeep tasks are undervalued suggests these duties may compete with other work unless they are funded. No study reports the staffing cost or the time burden of maintaining owner assignments at scale.

NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to define ownership of generative AI incident response, and CHAI guidance asks them to specify who is accountable and to whom. A multi-society radiology statement calls for named vendor contacts for error reporting. These are voluntary frameworks, and the supplied sources cite no binding federal or state requirement for named AI owners.

Several endorsing sources, including CHAI guidance, tie accountability to knowing whom end users should contact with concerns and who will act. The hazard studies suggest that such a contact is often missing today. No study has examined whether named owners make it easier for patients or clinicians to report a problem and reach a responsible person.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems lack studies that compare AI programs with and without named owners on measurable outcomes such as time to detect performance drift, time to resolve reported incidents, and completion rates for scheduled monitoring. Pre-post or stepped rollout designs across several systems could supply this evidence, along with data on staffing hours per owned solution.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither hazard study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tests the practice in any setting. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff available to fill six ownership roles, so the feasibility and effect of the practice in those settings remain unknown.
